top_choice_rationale: P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) recognises a bounded, mature discovery with a traceable credit trail: demand estimation with endogenous prices and realistic substitution patterns (Berry 1994; BLP 1995). It supplies both a new empirical capacity and a framework that recovers markups and counterfactual policy effects. Its identifying assumptions are explicit and have been probed in many applications, including merger retrospectives, and it is used well beyond industrial organisation. The cost is real: the three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan-Reiss and Benkard-Levin, and Pakes' share is likely larger than the others'. A narrow, paper-anchored citation on demand estimation handles this honestly. P001 (Kiyotaki-Moore pair) is a close second. It has equally clean originators and arguably wider conceptual reach, but direct identification of the specific collateral channel is more mixed and I weigh validated empirical record more. P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is third. The China-shock core is strong, but the technology and trade strands overlap with recent prizes, and the size and persistence of the effects and the shift-share inference are still debated. All three proposals are better than no award, so P000 is last. These are judgements of weighting from background knowledge, not verified citation data, and I do not count other members' support as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile for P002 or P001; my labour-economics field is near P003 (B023), and I presented the 2023 prize to Goldin, a known co-author of Katz (not in P003). My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any proposal. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
